heading: Thirty small kingdoms and a summer capital
body: Where most Indian states were built by consolidating power into one or two dominant kingdoms, Himachal Pradesh was built by leaving power scattered. On the eve of Indian independence, the territory that would become Himachal Pradesh was made up of around thirty princely states — plus one British-administered district — grouped loosely into the "Punjab Hill States" (including Mandi, Suket, Chamba and Bilaspur) and the "Shimla Hill States" (including Keonthal, Jubbal and Bushahr). Each ruled its own valley, minted its own identity, and struck its own terms with whichever larger power was ascendant at the time — first regional Rajput dynasties, then the Sikh Empire and Gurkha incursions from Nepal, and finally the British.

The British approach to these hill states was notably different from their approach to the plains: rather than annexing them outright, they governed most through a non-annexationist "Agency System", posting Political Agents or Residents to oversee local rulers who kept their thrones. What the British did claim outright was the high ground itself — quite literally. In 1864, Shimla, then a minor hill settlement, was declared the summer capital of British India, and the government of India relocated there for part of every year to escape the plains' heat; a railway line connecting Shimla to Kalka, engineered through the mountains, opened in 1903 specifically to serve that seasonal migration.

Independence did not immediately unify the hill states either. Himachal Pradesh was assembled in stages — the princely states first merged into a single administrative unit, Shimla itself passed to Punjab and then to Himachal, and it was only on 1 November 1966 that hill areas of Punjab, along with Kangra, Kullu, Shimla, and Lahaul & Spiti, were finally merged into the territory. Full statehood followed on 25 January 1971.

The map's Himachal entries reflect that fragmented past: the palaces and forts of individual hill kingdoms that ruled single valleys for centuries, and the colonial hill station built above all of them as a seasonal seat of an empire that governed from two capitals at once.
